name: Write in shorthand
blurb: Real shorthand — Gregg, Pitman or Teeline — takes months to reach reporting speed, but a few weeks gets you a personal note-taking system at 60 or 70 words per minute.
gear: A textbook for one system: Teeline is easiest for English
A smooth pen and lined paper
steps: Choose a system: Teeline is fastest to learn and used by journalists; Gregg and Pitman are faster at the top end but take longer.
Learn the alphabet strokes and the rules for joining them.
Learn the vowel rules — most systems reduce or omit vowels, which is where the speed comes from.
Learn the common word forms and abbreviations, which do most of the heavy lifting at speed.
Practise daily writing rather than reading — the skill is production.
Take dictation at graded speeds, starting at 40 words per minute and working upwards, and always practise reading your own notes back.
tips: Being unable to read your own shorthand is the standard failure. Practise transcription as much as writing.
Speed comes from word forms and phrasing, not from writing individual letters faster.
proof: You take dictation at 60 words per minute and transcribe it accurately an hour later.
